summary: BBN discusses connecting a host to an IMP over a long distance, beyond about 2000 feet and possibly tens of miles. Any good solution should have an extremely low undetected error rate, not be limited to low bandwidth, and let the host open multiple network conversations.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 263 describes a preliminary way to connect a host to an IMP over a long-distance link. It proposes full-duplex transmission, error checks and retransmission, while noting that detailed specifications were still being developed.

subtitle: A preliminary design for connecting hosts to an IMP over long distances.

tldr.problem: Some sites wanted to connect a host to an IMP over a cable or telephone circuit longer than the usual short-distance hard-wire connection.
tldr.mechanism: The preliminary design uses full-duplex Binary Synchronous transmission, block framing, a 24-bit CRC and positive-acknowledgment and timeout retransmission methods.
tldr.outcome: The RFC outlines an approach but says detailed design and documentation were not yet complete.

today: RFC 263 is a preliminary host-interface design published in December 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: Long-Distance Host Connections
sections.content:
The normal host connection placed an IMP at the host site and used a short hard-wire connection. BBN says some organizations wanted links longer than 2,000 feet, potentially tens of miles, using either cable or telephone circuits.

A suitable design should have an extremely low undetected error rate, avoid an inherently low bandwidth limit and preserve the host's ability to establish multiple network conversations.
sections.plainLanguage: Some hosts needed to connect to an IMP from far away. The link needed to be reliable, support useful bandwidth and preserve normal network conversations.

sections.title: Transmission and Error Checking
sections.content:
The preliminary proposal uses full-duplex transmission in the Binary Synchronous format already used for inter-IMP communication. The IMP end would frame blocks with special characters and add a 24-bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC); the host would provide matching formatting and checking.

The IMP and host would also use retransmission software based on positive acknowledgements and timeouts. The exact retransmission scheme was not yet fully defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends can send at once. They frame data in blocks, check each block for errors and use acknowledgements and timeouts to retransmit when needed.

sections.title: Host Requirements and Documentation
sections.content:
The host needs a front end to its NCP that can generate and check CRCs and provide simple retransmission logic. This could be implemented in software, special-purpose hardware, a minicomputer or another way chosen by the host organization.

BBN planned to document the design when complete, probably as an update to Report 1822. The RFC invites discussion while noting that detailed design was unfinished.
sections.plainLanguage: Each host must provide the data-formatting and error-checking functions at its end. BBN planned to publish full specifications after completing the design.
